Logging, detection and response
Last reviewed 2026-10-04 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can say which API events to record and which fields each one needs, keep credentials and attacker-supplied line breaks out of a log, write a detection rule over the events and state what it misses, and describe what happens after an alert in the terms NIST SP 800-61r3 uses.

Before you start. You should know the difference between authentication and authorization. The running example is the booking API from module 9, Object-level authorization, with its ownership check in place. Every other module in this course prevents an attack. This one is about noticing the attacks that prevention did not stop, and about being able to say afterwards what happened.
Published lesson 31 of 32Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExampleAir's booking API. A customer may read and cancel their own bookings. The ownership check from module 9 works: a request for someone else's booking gets 404 not found. Company names are fictional.

The account acct-77 asks for bkg-1001, then bkg-1002, and so on up to bkg-1040, one request a second. This is enumeration. Two of the forty bookings are its own. The other 38 requests are refused. The API logs successful reads only, so the log holds two lines for acct-77, and both look like a customer reading their own bookings. Nobody is told. The same account comes back tomorrow and tries the older API version, the export route and the invoice route, because module 9 showed that the check is often missing from one of them. The control did its job on every request, and the attack is still running.

The attack in this module is not a request that gets through. It is a refusal that nobody sees. The same thing happens at sign-in. An attacker makes one attempt on each of many accounts, using passwords leaked from another site (credential stuffing) or one common password (password spraying). Every attempt is refused, and a log that records only successful sign-ins shows nothing. Module 27, Attacks on authentication endpoints, is about the sign-in endpoint itself.

2. Why it works

Four broken assumptions:

  • "A refused request needs no record." A control that refuses a request answers the attacker and tells nobody else. OWASP Top 10:2025 A09 lists this exact case among its failures: auditable events "are not logged or logged inconsistently (for instance, only logging successful logins, but not failed attempts)". It states the result plainly: "Without logging and monitoring, attacks and breaches cannot be detected, and without alerting it is very difficult to respond quickly and effectively during a security incident."
  • "If something were wrong, someone would see it in the logs." A log is a file. It alerts nobody. NIST SP 800-92, written in September 2006 and still the final version, already described log analysis as work that is treated as low priority, and concluded: "Without sound processes for analyzing logs, the value of the logs is significantly reduced." A detection rule is the process that reads the log when no person does.
  • "We wrote the log, so we can trust what it says." Much of a log entry is copied from the request: the user name typed at sign-in, the identifier in the path, a header. If a value containing a line break is pasted into a line of text, the text after the break starts a new line, and a reader takes it for a second entry. That is log injection. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet says of event data that comes from another trust zone that "it must always be treated as untrusted data".
  • "More detail in the log is safer." A log is a copy of whatever you put in it, usually readable by more people and systems than the database it came from. A password or a token written to a log has been disclosed. Module 1, API keys, follows a key from a URL into a log and out to an attacker, and module 24, Data in model context, counts the places a prompt is copied to. This module does not repeat them. It adds the rule that makes both less likely: a logger that writes only the fields it was told to write.

A note on where this sits in the OWASP lists. The OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 has no entry for logging. The 2019 edition had one, titled API10:2019 Insufficient Logging & Monitoring, and the 2023 list of ten does not carry it. Among the ten 2023 entries, only API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows mentions it, in its list of references. The current OWASP entry on the subject is in the general web list: A09:2025 Security Logging & Alerting Failures. Do not cite the API Top 10 2023 for a logging finding.
3. The control
What to record

The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet has a list headed "Where possible, always log". For an API, these entries on it matter most:

  • Authentication successes and failures.
  • Authorization (access control) failures.
  • Input validation failures, which module 13, Request and response contracts, produces.
  • Session management failures, such as a token that fails validation.
  • Use of higher-risk functionality: user administration, use of administrative privileges, access to sensitive data, data import and export.
  • Suspicious business logic activity, such as an attempt to exceed a limit or to perform steps out of order. Module 11, Business flows and idempotency, names the flows.

The same cheat sheet warns against logging everything: "There is no one size fits all solution, and a blind checklist approach can lead to unnecessary "alarm fog" that means real problems go undetected."

The cheat sheet's summary of what each event needs is "when, where, who and what". It adds an interaction identifier, which links every event caused by one request. This course calls it a correlation ID. This is one event exactly as the lab writes it, a customer who mistyped one booking id:

{"appid": "exampleair.bookings", "datetime": "2026-10-04T09:00:05+00:00", "event": "authz_fail", "host": "api-1", "level": "CRITICAL", "reason": "not_owner", "request_id": "api-1-req-0002", "resource": "bkg-1003", "result": "fail", "route": "GET /bookings/{id}", "source_ip": "198.51.100.7", "userid": "acct-91"}

QuestionFieldsNotes
WhendatetimeThe clock of the host that wrote the event, in ISO 8601 with a UTC offset. The OWASP Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet asks for that format.
Whereappid, host, routeThe route is a fixed label, not the raw request target. Module 1 gives the reason.
Whouserid, source_ipThe authenticated account where there is one. At sign-in the user name is whatever the caller typed.
Whatevent, level, resource, result, reasonThe response to the caller was a plain 404. The reason stays in the log.
Which requestrequest_idThe same value goes in every event one request causes, and in the error response, so a support ticket can be matched to a log entry.

For agents, record three more things: which agent acted, on whose behalf, and which tool it called with which outcome. The OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet recommends: "Log all agent decisions, tool calls, and outcomes." The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 says under ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation: "Maintain immutable logs of all tool invocations and parameter changes." Recording the person an agent acted for is this project's reasoning, not a quotation: module 19, Delegation and token exchange, puts both identities in the token, and an event that keeps only one of them cannot answer who asked. Module 23, Agent authority and approvals, adds the approval that covered the call.
What never to write

The Logging Cheat Sheet lists data that "should usually not be recorded directly in the logs, but instead should be removed, masked, sanitized, hashed, or encrypted". The list includes session identification values, access tokens, authentication passwords, database connection strings, encryption keys and other primary secrets, bank account or payment card holder data, and sensitive personal data. An access token or an API key in a log is a working credential for anyone who can read the log.

The control is an allowlist of field names inside the logger. The application can pass anything. The logger writes the fields on its list and drops the rest. A pattern that hunts for secrets in text has to recognise every secret. A list of permitted fields does not.

The allowlist has a limit, and the lab measures it. It checks the name of a field, not what the field holds. If a client pastes a credential where the booking id goes, resource is an allowed field and the credential is written. So validate a value before logging it, and when validation fails, log the name of the field that failed and not the value.
How to write it

1. One event, one machine-readable record. Write each event as one JSON object on one line. This is structured logging. The JSON encoder turns a line break inside a value into the two characters \n, so a value cannot end the line it is written on. The Logging Cheat Sheet recommends both halves: "Perform sanitization on all event data to prevent log injection attacks e.g. carriage return (CR), line feed (LF) and delimiter characters", and "Encode data correctly for the output (logged) format".
  2. Use the encoder. Do not strip characters by hand. Removing line feeds from a text line leaves the delimiters. Exercise 2 shows a stripped line that no longer forges an entry and now blames the wrong user.
  3. Use one vocabulary. The OWASP Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet "proposes a standard vocabulary for logging security events", so that a rule can key on the same event name in every service. The lab uses four of its names: authn_login_success, authn_login_fail, authz_fail and input_validation_fail. The vocabulary writes the event and its parameters as one string, for example authz_fail:joebob1,resource. The lab keeps the name alone in event and puts the parameters in their own fields, so a comma or a colon inside a value cannot change what the event says. That split is this project's choice.
  4. A level is not an alert. The vocabulary gives authz_fail the level CRITICAL. A customer who mistypes one booking id produces one. Nobody should be paged for it. The level says how the event ranks. A rule decides whether anyone is told.
  5. Log names, not payloads. For an input that matched a SQL injection signature, the vocabulary warns: "Logging the payload is dangerous and may result in log injection." Record which rule matched and which parameter.
Rules that read the events

A detection rule is a condition over events, evaluated by a program. The lab has four. Each one is a count inside a time window:

  1. R1. Five authz_fail events for one userid inside 60 seconds. This catches the fast walk.
  2. R2. authn_login_fail events for five different userid values from one source_ip inside 300 seconds. A rule that counts failures per account never fires here, because each account fails once.
  3. R3. Ten booking_cancel events by one userid inside 300 seconds. Every one of those requests is allowed. This rule reads successes, because abuse of a business flow produces no refusal.
  4. R4. Ten authz_fail events for one userid inside 24 hours. This is R1 with a long window, for the walk that goes slowly.

The numbers are this lab's, chosen to make the output easy to read. Yours come from your own traffic. Section 4 says how to change them.
Protect the log

1. Integrity. An attacker who gets onto the host can edit the log. The Logging Cheat Sheet recommends, for logs at rest: "Build in tamper detection so you know if a record has been modified or deleted" and "Store or copy log data to read-only media as soon as possible". NIST SP 800-92 section 5.1.3 says protecting archived log files "could include creating and securing message digests for the files". A message digest is a hash.
  2. Access. NIST SP 800-92 section 5.1.3: "Users should not have any access to most log files unless some level of access is necessary for creating log entries. If so, users should have append-only privileges and no read access if possible." The cheat sheet adds that "All access to the logs must be recorded and monitored".
  3. Retention. The cheat sheet says log data "must not be destroyed before the duration of the required data retention period, and must not be kept beyond this time". It gives no number. NIST SP 800-92 gives examples only: Table 4-1 shows 1 to 2 weeks for low impact systems, 1 to 3 months for moderate impact systems and 3 to 12 months for high impact systems, and the text beside it says "Organizations should not adopt these values as-is". The period comes from your legal and contractual duties and from how late you expect to find out about an attack.
  4. Time. A rule that counts events in a window depends on timestamps from different hosts meaning the same thing. The executive summary of NIST SP 800-92 lists among administrators' responsibilities "Ensuring that each logging host's clock is synched to a common time source". Checks 44 and 45 of the lab show a rule going blind when one clock is two minutes out.
After the alert

An alert is the start of work, not the end. NIST SP 800-61r3 (April 2025) is the current NIST publication on incident response, and it changed the model. Its predecessor drew a cycle of four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. Revision 3 calls that the previous model and organises its recommendations around the six Functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 instead: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. In its words, "Govern, Identify, and Protect help organizations prevent some incidents, prepare to handle incidents that do occur, reduce the impact of those incidents", and "Detect, Respond, and Recover help organizations discover, manage, prioritize, contain, eradicate, and recover from cybersecurity incidents". Lessons learned are no longer a last phase. They belong to the Improvement Category of Identify and feed every Function at any time.

The document does not make its model mandatory. It says: "Organizations should use the incident response life cycle framework or model that suits them best." Each row of its Table 3 is a CSF 2.0 outcome with recommendations, considerations or notes beside it. For the enumeration alert in this module, the rows read like this:

  1. Detect. Events are monitored, analysed and correlated. The outcome DE.AE-08 is that an incident is declared "when adverse events meet the defined incident criteria". An alert is not yet an incident: someone, or some rule with written criteria, decides.
  2. Respond: triage. "Perform a preliminary review of a new incident report to verify that a cybersecurity incident has occurred, then estimate the severity of the incident and the level of urgency needed to respond to it" (RS.MA-02).
  3. Respond: analyse. "Determine the sequence of events that have occurred during the incident and which assets and resources were involved in each of those events" (RS.AN-03). This is the step the log exists for. Checks 16 and 17 of the lab do it: 38 identifiers refused, and three of them real bookings of other customers.
  4. Respond: contain. Stop it spreading (the outcome RS.MI-01, incidents are contained). Here that means suspending the account or its credential, and checking every other route that reaches a booking for the same account.
  5. Recover and improve. Restore what was affected. Feed back what you learn as soon as you learn it, not only at the end: a missing check found, a rule added, a threshold changed.

5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: an event in the log shows that the application made that decision, for that account, at the time on that host's clock. An alert shows that the condition in one rule was met.

Doesn't prove nothing happened. No alert means no rule fired. In check 42 a walk split across ten accounts and ten addresses produces 30 logged refusals and no alert from R1 or R4. Every count-in-a-window rule has a rate below which it is silent. Lengthen the window and the attacker slows down again. Say "no rule fired", never "no attack".

Doesn't prove who. userid is the account that authenticated. If its credential was stolen, the log names the victim. Before authentication, as at sign-in, the user name is whatever the caller typed.

Doesn't prove the log is complete. Whoever can write the log can remove lines from it. A hash chain makes an edit visible only to someone holding a digest the attacker could not rewrite (checks 49 and 50). The Logging Cheat Sheet is frank about the general case: non-repudiation "is hard to achieve for logs because their trustworthiness is often just based on the logging party being audited properly".

Doesn't mean every alert is an attack. A false positive is an alert for activity that was not an attack. A09:2025 names the cost: "Too many false positive alerts make it impossible to distinguish important alerts from unimportant ones". NIST SP 800-61r3 recommends: "Tune the continuous monitoring technologies to reduce false positives and false negatives to acceptable levels."

Detection is not prevention. The 40 requests in the lab all reach the API. Logging them refuses nothing and slows nothing down. A rate limit does that, in module 15, Rate limiting and cost controls. And an alert about a refused walk is a reason to go and look for the route where the check is missing, not evidence that there is none.
6. Prove it

A working implementation must pass every one of these. If any fails, the control is broken:

  • A request refused by an authorization check leaves an event with the account, the object, the route and a request id. Test the refusal, not the success.
  • A failed sign-in leaves an event. So does a request that fails input validation.
  • A user name containing a line feed, a carriage return or the log's own delimiter produces exactly one log entry, and the entry parses back to the value that was sent.
  • A generated test password, sent to the sign-in endpoint and refused, appears nowhere in the application log, the gateway log or the error tracker.
  • A generated test token pasted into an identifier field appears nowhere in the log.
  • Replaying the fast walk in a test environment raises exactly one alert, for the right account.
  • Replaying one mistyped identifier raises none.
  • Replaying the walk slowly, below the fast rule, raises the slow rule's alert. Write down the rate below which nothing fires.
  • Deleting or editing one line of a stored log is detected by a check that runs somewhere the application cannot write.
  • Two hosts that log the same burst produce timestamps that agree to within the rule's window.

Download labs/detection_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3. The API, the two loggers and the rules are plain Python objects. Nothing opens a socket or writes a file, and time is a counter the lab advances by hand, so the output is the same on every run. Eight results are worth reading closely. Checks 3 to 6 are the attack: 38 refusals, four lines in the log, none of them a refusal, and an investigator who asks what acct-77 did is shown two of its own bookings. Checks 11 to 15 are the same traffic with events: one alert, for the right account, seven requests into the walk, and none for the customer whose one mistake is in the same log at the same level. Check 17 is something only the log knows. The API answered 404 for all 38, and the events still separate the three identifiers that belong to other customers from the 35 that do not exist, which is the list an incident responder needs first.

Checks 19 to 21 show why the choice of key matters. Each of the six accounts fails once, so a rule counting failures per account sees nothing, and the rule counting different accounts per address fires. Checks 22 and 23 are the rule over successes: twelve cancellations, no refusal anywhere, one alert.

Checks 35 to 37 are the limit of the allowlist from section 3, and checks 42 and 43 are the limit of the rules: a split walk that nothing catches, next to an honest batch client that R1 does catch. Checks 44 and 45 are the same six requests with and without a two-minute clock error.

8. Check your understanding

The API already refuses every request for another customer's booking. Why log the refusals?

Because a refusal tells only the attacker. The walk in the lab is refused 38 times and leaves nothing in a log of successes, so it can continue against every other route until it finds one where the check is missing. The refusals are also the record an investigation starts from: which account, which identifiers, from when to when.

The vocabulary gives authz_fail the level CRITICAL. Should each one page the on-call engineer?

No. The level ranks the event. A customer who mistypes one booking id produces a CRITICAL event, and check 15 shows no alert for them. A rule over the events decides whether a person is told: here, five for one account inside 60 seconds.

A colleague fixes log injection by deleting line feeds from user names before logging. What is left?

The delimiters, and every other character a reader treats as a line break. Exercise 2 measures both: the forged entry disappears, the real entry now names the wrong user, and a carriage return forges the entry again. The fix is an encoder for the output format, such as one JSON object per line, not a list of characters to remove.

No alert fired last month. What can you report?

That none of your rules fired, along with which rules they are and the rate below which each is silent. Check 42 logs 30 refusals and raises no alert. "No alerts" is a statement about the rules. It is not a statement about attackers.

Quick check

A walk that leaves no trace

An API returns 404 for any booking the caller does not own, and logs successful reads only. One account requests 40 booking ids in 40 seconds, and 38 are refused. What does the log show for that account?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/detection_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The lab compares every result with the one it expects, so each of these edits also makes it exit 1 and list what differed. Two answers carry a measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. Someone adds password to the allowlist

A developer wants to see what users type when sign-in fails. In ALLOWED_FIELDS, add "password" after "host". Nothing else changes.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Encoding is not hiding. JSON escapes quotes and line breaks so the value cannot break the line. The value itself is written in full, and check 33 finds it.
  • Check 32 already prints True. The plain logger has no allowlist and wrote the password before this edit.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 33 goes from False to True: the password a user typed is now in the JSON log. Check 34 goes from ['password'] to []: the allowlist drops nothing, because the one thing it was dropping has been allowed. One word in one tuple undoes the control, which is why check log-03 in the Reference layer asks for a test with a generated value and not a review of the list.
  • Check 9 still prints the same twelve field names. The API passes password only from the failed sign-in path, so an authz_fail event never had one to write.

2. The plain logger strips line feeds

Someone fixes Part C without changing the format. In PlainLogger.emit, replace fields[name] with a version that turns each line feed into a space:

pairs = " ".join("%s=%s" % (name, str(fields[name]).replace("\n", " "))
                 for name in sorted(fields))
What do checks 25 to 27 print?

Every option, and why
  • The line feed is gone, so the text can no longer start a second line. Check 25 goes from 2 to 1 and check 27, the forged sign-in for admin, goes from 1 to 0.
  • That is the result the edit was meant to produce. The forged text is still inside the line, after the real user name, and it is made of name=value pairs. A reader that splits on spaces takes the last value it sees for each name.
  • Correct. Exit 1, three failures. Check 25 goes from 2 to 1, check 26 from authn_login_success for admin to authn_login_fail for admin, and check 27 from 1 to 0. The forged success is gone. The one real entry now says the failed sign-in was for admin. Measured on the parsed event: its userid is admin, its result is success and its source_ip is 198.51.100.7, the customer's address, where the request came from 203.0.113.50. The Logging Cheat Sheet lists this among attacks on logs: "An attacker causes the wrong identity to be logged in order to conceal the responsible party." Also measured, on a user name the lab does not send: with a carriage return where the line feed was, the edited logger writes two lines again and the reader counts one successful sign-in for admin, because the reader splits on more than line feeds. The JSON logger writes one line for either user name and reads the same value back. Check log-04 in the Reference layer asks for an encoder for this reason.
  • The plain logger never drops an event unless successes_only is set, and Part C does not set it.

3. The threshold is raised to quiet a false positive

Check 43 is a false positive: an honest batch client trips R1. To stop it, change threshold=5 to threshold=7 in the line that defines R1.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 43 does go from ['acct-agency'] to []. Three other checks use R1 with traffic close to the old threshold, and they move too.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 43 goes from ['acct-agency'] to [], which was the aim. Check 12 goes from 2026-10-04T09:00:17+00:00 to 2026-10-04T09:00:19+00:00 and check 13 from 7 to 9: the fast walk is still caught, two requests later. Check 45 goes from ['acct-77'] to []: the burst of six refusals through two hosts is now under the threshold, so a real attack is missed with both clocks correct. One number moved a false positive and a true positive together. Check log-06 in the Reference layer asks for the attack to be replayed after every threshold change for this reason.
  • Check 11 still prints ['acct-77']. The walk produces 38 refusals at one a second, far more than seven in a minute.
  • Check 15 still prints 0. One refusal is below a threshold of five and below a threshold of seven.

4. The clock error is 30 seconds, not 120

In Part E, check 44 runs six refusals through two hosts with the second host's clock 120 seconds fast. Change two_hosts(120) to two_hosts(30) in that check.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The rule does not need the clocks to agree exactly. It needs the error to be small next to the window.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 44 goes from [] to ['acct-77']. With a 30 second error all six timestamps still fall inside one 60 second window, so R1 fires. Measured on values the lab does not use: an error of 56 seconds still raises the alert and 57 seconds does not. The lab's own label still says 120 s, which is why the run fails. Check log-09 in the Reference layer ties the allowed clock error to the shortest window any rule uses.
  • Check 45 calls two_hosts(0) and this edit does not touch it. It still prints ['acct-77'].
  • Only check 44 was edited, and check 45 has no clock error to change.

It is guidance and sets no requirement.
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Event attributes, says each event records "when, where, who and what", and describes an interaction identifier as "a method of linking all (relevant) events for a single user interaction".
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Data to exclude, says session identification values, access tokens, authentication passwords, database connection strings, encryption keys and other primary secrets, payment card holder data and sensitive personal data "should usually not be recorded directly in the logs, but instead should be removed, masked, sanitized, hashed, or encrypted".

It gives authn_login_success the level INFO, authn_login_fail and input_validation_fail the level WARN, and authz_fail the level CRITICAL, and says all dates "should be logged in ISO 8601 format WITH UTC offset". It is a proposal, not a standard.

  • OptionHoneytokens: records or identities that no real user touches, so that any access to them is an alert with almost no false positives. OWASP Top 10:2025 A09 suggests them.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• Refusals are logged, not only successes Every failed sign-in, authorization failure and input validation failure leaves an event. Test by sending a request that is refused and reading the log.
  • Each event says when, where, who and what, and carries a request id Timestamp, application, host, route, account, source address, event name, object, result and reason. The request id also appears in the error response.
  • No credential, token or session identifier is written to any log The logger has an allowlist of field names. Test with a generated password and a generated token on the failure paths, then search every log for them.
  • A logged value cannot forge or alter an entry Events are written by an encoder for a structured format. Test a value containing a line feed, a carriage return and the delimiter, and parse the log back.
  • Event names and levels come from one documented vocabulary Every service uses the same name for the same event, so one rule covers all of them.
  • Detection rules read the events, and each is tested by replaying the attack At least refusals per account, different accounts failing from one source, and a count on each sensitive business flow. Replay after every threshold change.
  • The slow and the distributed variants have been considered A long-window rule exists, and the rate below which no rule fires is written down.
  • Logs are protected from the systems that write them Append-only or copied off the host promptly, read access restricted and itself logged, and a retention period defined for each log type.
  • Clocks are synchronised to a common source The allowed clock error is smaller than the shortest window any rule uses. Timestamps carry a UTC offset.
  • An alert reaches a person who has a written procedure The procedure covers triage, the criteria for declaring an incident, reconstruction from the log, containment and what to record. It has been exercised.

intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can say which API events to record and which fields each one needs, keep credentials and attacker-supplied line breaks out of a log, write a detection rule over the events and state what it misses, and describe what happens after an alert in the terms NIST SP 800-61r3 uses.

Before you start. You should know the difference between authentication and authorization. The running example is the booking API from module 9, Object-level authorization, with its ownership check in place. Every other module in this course prevents an attack. This one is about noticing the attacks that prevention did not stop, and about being able to say afterwards what happened.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExampleAir's booking API. A customer may read and cancel their own bookings. The ownership check from module 9 works: a request for someone else's booking gets 404 not found. Company names are fictional.

The account acct-77 asks for bkg-1001, then bkg-1002, and so on up to bkg-1040, one request a second. This is enumeration. Two of the forty bookings are its own. The other 38 requests are refused. The API logs successful reads only, so the log holds two lines for acct-77, and both look like a customer reading their own bookings. Nobody is told. The same account comes back tomorrow and tries the older API version, the export route and the invoice route, because module 9 showed that the check is often missing from one of them. The control did its job on every request, and the attack is still running.

The attack in this module is not a request that gets through. It is a refusal that nobody sees. The same thing happens at sign-in. An attacker makes one attempt on each of many accounts, using passwords leaked from another site (credential stuffing) or one common password (password spraying). Every attempt is refused, and a log that records only successful sign-ins shows nothing. Module 27, Attacks on authentication endpoints, is about the sign-in endpoint itself.

What the attacker doesLog records successes onlyFailures are logged, no rule reads themFailures are logged, rules read them
Walks 40 booking ids in 40 seconds from one accountUnseen: 2 lines, both ordinaryRecorded, 38 refusals. Unseen until someone looksAlert after the fifth refusal
Tries one wrong password on each of six accounts from one addressUnseenRecorded. Unseen until someone looksAlert on five different accounts from one address
Cancels twelve bookings in 24 seconds, every one allowedRecorded as twelve successes. UnseenRecorded as twelve successes. UnseenAlert on ten cancellations by one account
Walks 30 ids, one every 20 minutesUnseenRecorded. Unseen until someone looksMissed by the 60-second rule. Alert from the 24-hour rule
Splits the same slow walk across ten accounts and ten addressesUnseenRecorded. Unseen until someone looksNo alert from any rule here

The last row never turns green. Section 5 says why, and what that means for how much you can claim.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Four broken assumptions:

  • "A refused request needs no record." A control that refuses a request answers the attacker and tells nobody else. OWASP Top 10:2025 A09 lists this exact case among its failures: auditable events "are not logged or logged inconsistently (for instance, only logging successful logins, but not failed attempts)". It states the result plainly: "Without logging and monitoring, attacks and breaches cannot be detected, and without alerting it is very difficult to respond quickly and effectively during a security incident."
  • "If something were wrong, someone would see it in the logs." A log is a file. It alerts nobody. NIST SP 800-92, written in September 2006 and still the final version, already described log analysis as work that is treated as low priority, and concluded: "Without sound processes for analyzing logs, the value of the logs is significantly reduced." A detection rule is the process that reads the log when no person does.
  • "We wrote the log, so we can trust what it says." Much of a log entry is copied from the request: the user name typed at sign-in, the identifier in the path, a header. If a value containing a line break is pasted into a line of text, the text after the break starts a new line, and a reader takes it for a second entry. That is log injection. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet says of event data that comes from another trust zone that "it must always be treated as untrusted data".
  • "More detail in the log is safer." A log is a copy of whatever you put in it, usually readable by more people and systems than the database it came from. A password or a token written to a log has been disclosed. Module 1, API keys, follows a key from a URL into a log and out to an attacker, and module 24, Data in model context, counts the places a prompt is copied to. This module does not repeat them. It adds the rule that makes both less likely: a logger that writes only the fields it was told to write.

A note on where this sits in the OWASP lists. The OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 has no entry for logging. The 2019 edition had one, titled API10:2019 Insufficient Logging & Monitoring, and the 2023 list of ten does not carry it. Among the ten 2023 entries, only API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows mentions it, in its list of references. The current OWASP entry on the subject is in the general web list: A09:2025 Security Logging & Alerting Failures. Do not cite the API Top 10 2023 for a logging finding.

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
What to record

The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet has a list headed "Where possible, always log". For an API, these entries on it matter most:

  • Authentication successes and failures.
  • Authorization (access control) failures.
  • Input validation failures, which module 13, Request and response contracts, produces.
  • Session management failures, such as a token that fails validation.
  • Use of higher-risk functionality: user administration, use of administrative privileges, access to sensitive data, data import and export.
  • Suspicious business logic activity, such as an attempt to exceed a limit or to perform steps out of order. Module 11, Business flows and idempotency, names the flows.

The same cheat sheet warns against logging everything: "There is no one size fits all solution, and a blind checklist approach can lead to unnecessary "alarm fog" that means real problems go undetected."

The cheat sheet's summary of what each event needs is "when, where, who and what". It adds an interaction identifier, which links every event caused by one request. This course calls it a correlation ID. This is one event exactly as the lab writes it, a customer who mistyped one booking id:

{"appid": "exampleair.bookings", "datetime": "2026-10-04T09:00:05+00:00", "event": "authz_fail", "host": "api-1", "level": "CRITICAL", "reason": "not_owner", "request_id": "api-1-req-0002", "resource": "bkg-1003", "result": "fail", "route": "GET /bookings/{id}", "source_ip": "198.51.100.7", "userid": "acct-91"}
QuestionFieldsNotes
WhendatetimeThe clock of the host that wrote the event, in ISO 8601 with a UTC offset. The OWASP Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet asks for that format.
Whereappid, host, routeThe route is a fixed label, not the raw request target. Module 1 gives the reason.
Whouserid, source_ipThe authenticated account where there is one. At sign-in the user name is whatever the caller typed.
Whatevent, level, resource, result, reasonThe response to the caller was a plain 404. The reason stays in the log.
Which requestrequest_idThe same value goes in every event one request causes, and in the error response, so a support ticket can be matched to a log entry.

For agents, record three more things: which agent acted, on whose behalf, and which tool it called with which outcome. The OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet recommends: "Log all agent decisions, tool calls, and outcomes." The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 says under ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation: "Maintain immutable logs of all tool invocations and parameter changes." Recording the person an agent acted for is this project's reasoning, not a quotation: module 19, Delegation and token exchange, puts both identities in the token, and an event that keeps only one of them cannot answer who asked. Module 23, Agent authority and approvals, adds the approval that covered the call.

What never to write

The Logging Cheat Sheet lists data that "should usually not be recorded directly in the logs, but instead should be removed, masked, sanitized, hashed, or encrypted". The list includes session identification values, access tokens, authentication passwords, database connection strings, encryption keys and other primary secrets, bank account or payment card holder data, and sensitive personal data. An access token or an API key in a log is a working credential for anyone who can read the log.

The control is an allowlist of field names inside the logger. The application can pass anything. The logger writes the fields on its list and drops the rest. A pattern that hunts for secrets in text has to recognise every secret. A list of permitted fields does not.

The allowlist has a limit, and the lab measures it. It checks the name of a field, not what the field holds. If a client pastes a credential where the booking id goes, resource is an allowed field and the credential is written. So validate a value before logging it, and when validation fails, log the name of the field that failed and not the value.

How to write it

  1. One event, one machine-readable record. Write each event as one JSON object on one line. This is structured logging. The JSON encoder turns a line break inside a value into the two characters \n, so a value cannot end the line it is written on. The Logging Cheat Sheet recommends both halves: "Perform sanitization on all event data to prevent log injection attacks e.g. carriage return (CR), line feed (LF) and delimiter characters", and "Encode data correctly for the output (logged) format".
  2. Use the encoder. Do not strip characters by hand. Removing line feeds from a text line leaves the delimiters. Exercise 2 shows a stripped line that no longer forges an entry and now blames the wrong user.
  3. Use one vocabulary. The OWASP Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet "proposes a standard vocabulary for logging security events", so that a rule can key on the same event name in every service. The lab uses four of its names: authn_login_success, authn_login_fail, authz_fail and input_validation_fail. The vocabulary writes the event and its parameters as one string, for example authz_fail:joebob1,resource. The lab keeps the name alone in event and puts the parameters in their own fields, so a comma or a colon inside a value cannot change what the event says. That split is this project's choice.
  4. A level is not an alert. The vocabulary gives authz_fail the level CRITICAL. A customer who mistypes one booking id produces one. Nobody should be paged for it. The level says how the event ranks. A rule decides whether anyone is told.
  5. Log names, not payloads. For an input that matched a SQL injection signature, the vocabulary warns: "Logging the payload is dangerous and may result in log injection." Record which rule matched and which parameter.

Rules that read the events

A detection rule is a condition over events, evaluated by a program. The lab has four. Each one is a count inside a time window:

  1. R1. Five authz_fail events for one userid inside 60 seconds. This catches the fast walk.
  2. R2. authn_login_fail events for five different userid values from one source_ip inside 300 seconds. A rule that counts failures per account never fires here, because each account fails once.
  3. R3. Ten booking_cancel events by one userid inside 300 seconds. Every one of those requests is allowed. This rule reads successes, because abuse of a business flow produces no refusal.
  4. R4. Ten authz_fail events for one userid inside 24 hours. This is R1 with a long window, for the walk that goes slowly.

The numbers are this lab's, chosen to make the output easy to read. Yours come from your own traffic. Section 4 says how to change them.

Protect the log

  1. Integrity. An attacker who gets onto the host can edit the log. The Logging Cheat Sheet recommends, for logs at rest: "Build in tamper detection so you know if a record has been modified or deleted" and "Store or copy log data to read-only media as soon as possible". NIST SP 800-92 section 5.1.3 says protecting archived log files "could include creating and securing message digests for the files". A message digest is a hash.
  2. Access. NIST SP 800-92 section 5.1.3: "Users should not have any access to most log files unless some level of access is necessary for creating log entries. If so, users should have append-only privileges and no read access if possible." The cheat sheet adds that "All access to the logs must be recorded and monitored".
  3. Retention. The cheat sheet says log data "must not be destroyed before the duration of the required data retention period, and must not be kept beyond this time". It gives no number. NIST SP 800-92 gives examples only: Table 4-1 shows 1 to 2 weeks for low impact systems, 1 to 3 months for moderate impact systems and 3 to 12 months for high impact systems, and the text beside it says "Organizations should not adopt these values as-is". The period comes from your legal and contractual duties and from how late you expect to find out about an attack.
  4. Time. A rule that counts events in a window depends on timestamps from different hosts meaning the same thing. The executive summary of NIST SP 800-92 lists among administrators' responsibilities "Ensuring that each logging host's clock is synched to a common time source". Checks 44 and 45 of the lab show a rule going blind when one clock is two minutes out.

After the alert

An alert is the start of work, not the end. NIST SP 800-61r3 (April 2025) is the current NIST publication on incident response, and it changed the model. Its predecessor drew a cycle of four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. Revision 3 calls that the previous model and organises its recommendations around the six Functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 instead: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. In its words, "Govern, Identify, and Protect help organizations prevent some incidents, prepare to handle incidents that do occur, reduce the impact of those incidents", and "Detect, Respond, and Recover help organizations discover, manage, prioritize, contain, eradicate, and recover from cybersecurity incidents". Lessons learned are no longer a last phase. They belong to the Improvement Category of Identify and feed every Function at any time.

The document does not make its model mandatory. It says: "Organizations should use the incident response life cycle framework or model that suits them best." Each row of its Table 3 is a CSF 2.0 outcome with recommendations, considerations or notes beside it. For the enumeration alert in this module, the rows read like this:

  1. Detect. Events are monitored, analysed and correlated. The outcome DE.AE-08 is that an incident is declared "when adverse events meet the defined incident criteria". An alert is not yet an incident: someone, or some rule with written criteria, decides.
  2. Respond: triage. "Perform a preliminary review of a new incident report to verify that a cybersecurity incident has occurred, then estimate the severity of the incident and the level of urgency needed to respond to it" (RS.MA-02).
  3. Respond: analyse. "Determine the sequence of events that have occurred during the incident and which assets and resources were involved in each of those events" (RS.AN-03). This is the step the log exists for. Checks 16 and 17 of the lab do it: 38 identifiers refused, and three of them real bookings of other customers.
  4. Respond: contain. Stop it spreading (the outcome RS.MI-01, incidents are contained). Here that means suspending the account or its credential, and checking every other route that reaches a booking for the same account.
  5. Recover and improve. Restore what was affected. Feed back what you learn as soon as you learn it, not only at the end: a missing check found, a rule added, a threshold changed.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: an event in the log shows that the application made that decision, for that account, at the time on that host's clock. An alert shows that the condition in one rule was met.

Doesn't prove nothing happened. No alert means no rule fired. In check 42 a walk split across ten accounts and ten addresses produces 30 logged refusals and no alert from R1 or R4. Every count-in-a-window rule has a rate below which it is silent. Lengthen the window and the attacker slows down again. Say "no rule fired", never "no attack".

Doesn't prove who. userid is the account that authenticated. If its credential was stolen, the log names the victim. Before authentication, as at sign-in, the user name is whatever the caller typed.

Doesn't prove the log is complete. Whoever can write the log can remove lines from it. A hash chain makes an edit visible only to someone holding a digest the attacker could not rewrite (checks 49 and 50). The Logging Cheat Sheet is frank about the general case: non-repudiation "is hard to achieve for logs because their trustworthiness is often just based on the logging party being audited properly".

Doesn't mean every alert is an attack. A false positive is an alert for activity that was not an attack. A09:2025 names the cost: "Too many false positive alerts make it impossible to distinguish important alerts from unimportant ones". NIST SP 800-61r3 recommends: "Tune the continuous monitoring technologies to reduce false positives and false negatives to acceptable levels."

Detection is not prevention. The 40 requests in the lab all reach the API. Logging them refuses nothing and slows nothing down. A rate limit does that, in module 15, Rate limiting and cost controls. And an alert about a refused walk is a reason to go and look for the route where the check is missing, not evidence that there is none.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A working implementation must pass every one of these. If any fails, the control is broken:

  • A request refused by an authorization check leaves an event with the account, the object, the route and a request id. Test the refusal, not the success.
  • A failed sign-in leaves an event. So does a request that fails input validation.
  • A user name containing a line feed, a carriage return or the log's own delimiter produces exactly one log entry, and the entry parses back to the value that was sent.
  • A generated test password, sent to the sign-in endpoint and refused, appears nowhere in the application log, the gateway log or the error tracker.
  • A generated test token pasted into an identifier field appears nowhere in the log.
  • Replaying the fast walk in a test environment raises exactly one alert, for the right account.
  • Replaying one mistyped identifier raises none.
  • Replaying the walk slowly, below the fast rule, raises the slow rule's alert. Write down the rate below which nothing fires.
  • Deleting or editing one line of a stored log is detected by a check that runs somewhere the application cannot write.
  • Two hosts that log the same burst produce timestamps that agree to within the rule's window.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
The API already refuses every request for another customer's booking. Why log the refusals?

Because a refusal tells only the attacker. The walk in the lab is refused 38 times and leaves nothing in a log of successes, so it can continue against every other route until it finds one where the check is missing. The refusals are also the record an investigation starts from: which account, which identifiers, from when to when.

The vocabulary gives authz_fail the level CRITICAL. Should each one page the on-call engineer?

No. The level ranks the event. A customer who mistypes one booking id produces a CRITICAL event, and check 15 shows no alert for them. A rule over the events decides whether a person is told: here, five for one account inside 60 seconds.

A colleague fixes log injection by deleting line feeds from user names before logging. What is left?

The delimiters, and every other character a reader treats as a line break. Exercise 2 measures both: the forged entry disappears, the real entry now names the wrong user, and a carriage return forges the entry again. The fix is an encoder for the output format, such as one JSON object per line, not a list of characters to remove.

No alert fired last month. What can you report?

That none of your rules fired, along with which rules they are and the rate below which each is silent. Check 42 logs 30 refusals and raises no alert. "No alerts" is a statement about the rules. It is not a statement about attackers.

sections.heading: A walk that leaves no trace
sections.heading_text: A walk that leaves no trace
sections.html:
An API returns 404 for any booking the caller does not own, and logs successful reads only. One account requests 40 booking ids in 40 seconds, and 38 are refused. What does the log show for that account?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/detection_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The lab compares every result with the one it expects, so each of these edits also makes it exit 1 and list what differed. Two answers carry a measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. Someone adds password to the allowlist

A developer wants to see what users type when sign-in fails. In ALLOWED_FIELDS, add "password" after "host". Nothing else changes.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Encoding is not hiding. JSON escapes quotes and line breaks so the value cannot break the line. The value itself is written in full, and check 33 finds it.
  • Check 32 already prints True. The plain logger has no allowlist and wrote the password before this edit.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 33 goes from False to True: the password a user typed is now in the JSON log. Check 34 goes from ['password'] to []: the allowlist drops nothing, because the one thing it was dropping has been allowed. One word in one tuple undoes the control, which is why check log-03 in the Reference layer asks for a test with a generated value and not a review of the list.
  • Check 9 still prints the same twelve field names. The API passes password only from the failed sign-in path, so an authz_fail event never had one to write.

2. The plain logger strips line feeds

Someone fixes Part C without changing the format. In PlainLogger.emit, replace fields[name] with a version that turns each line feed into a space:

pairs = " ".join("%s=%s" % (name, str(fields[name]).replace("\n", " "))
                 for name in sorted(fields))
What do checks 25 to 27 print?

Every option, and why
  • The line feed is gone, so the text can no longer start a second line. Check 25 goes from 2 to 1 and check 27, the forged sign-in for admin, goes from 1 to 0.
  • That is the result the edit was meant to produce. The forged text is still inside the line, after the real user name, and it is made of name=value pairs. A reader that splits on spaces takes the last value it sees for each name.
  • Correct. Exit 1, three failures. Check 25 goes from 2 to 1, check 26 from authn_login_success for admin to authn_login_fail for admin, and check 27 from 1 to 0. The forged success is gone. The one real entry now says the failed sign-in was for admin. Measured on the parsed event: its userid is admin, its result is success and its source_ip is 198.51.100.7, the customer's address, where the request came from 203.0.113.50. The Logging Cheat Sheet lists this among attacks on logs: "An attacker causes the wrong identity to be logged in order to conceal the responsible party." Also measured, on a user name the lab does not send: with a carriage return where the line feed was, the edited logger writes two lines again and the reader counts one successful sign-in for admin, because the reader splits on more than line feeds. The JSON logger writes one line for either user name and reads the same value back. Check log-04 in the Reference layer asks for an encoder for this reason.
  • The plain logger never drops an event unless successes_only is set, and Part C does not set it.

3. The threshold is raised to quiet a false positive

Check 43 is a false positive: an honest batch client trips R1. To stop it, change threshold=5 to threshold=7 in the line that defines R1.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 43 does go from ['acct-agency'] to []. Three other checks use R1 with traffic close to the old threshold, and they move too.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 43 goes from ['acct-agency'] to [], which was the aim. Check 12 goes from 2026-10-04T09:00:17+00:00 to 2026-10-04T09:00:19+00:00 and check 13 from 7 to 9: the fast walk is still caught, two requests later. Check 45 goes from ['acct-77'] to []: the burst of six refusals through two hosts is now under the threshold, so a real attack is missed with both clocks correct. One number moved a false positive and a true positive together. Check log-06 in the Reference layer asks for the attack to be replayed after every threshold change for this reason.
  • Check 11 still prints ['acct-77']. The walk produces 38 refusals at one a second, far more than seven in a minute.
  • Check 15 still prints 0. One refusal is below a threshold of five and below a threshold of seven.

4. The clock error is 30 seconds, not 120

In Part E, check 44 runs six refusals through two hosts with the second host's clock 120 seconds fast. Change two_hosts(120) to two_hosts(30) in that check.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The rule does not need the clocks to agree exactly. It needs the error to be small next to the window.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 44 goes from [] to ['acct-77']. With a 30 second error all six timestamps still fall inside one 60 second window, so R1 fires. Measured on values the lab does not use: an error of 56 seconds still raises the alert and 57 seconds does not. The lab's own label still says 120 s, which is why the run fails. Check log-09 in the Reference layer ties the allowed clock error to the shortest window any rule uses.
  • Check 45 calls two_hosts(0) and this edit does not touch it. It still prints ['acct-77'].
  • Only check 44 was edited, and check 45 has no clock error to change.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Which events to log, recommends always logging, where possible, input validation failures, authentication successes and failures, authorization (access control) failures, session management failures, application errors and system events, use of higher-risk functionality, and suspicious business logic activities. It is guidance and sets no requirement.
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Event attributes, says each event records "when, where, who and what", and describes an interaction identifier as "a method of linking all (relevant) events for a single user interaction".
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Data to exclude, says session identification values, access tokens, authentication passwords, database connection strings, encryption keys and other primary secrets, payment card holder data and sensitive personal data "should usually not be recorded directly in the logs, but instead should be removed, masked, sanitized, hashed, or encrypted".
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Event collection, recommends sanitizing all event data "to prevent log injection attacks e.g. carriage return (CR), line feed (LF) and delimiter characters", encoding data correctly for the logged format, and synchronizing time "across all servers and devices".
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet, under Protection, recommends tamper detection, copying log data to read-only media as soon as possible, recording and monitoring all access to the logs, and restricting the privileges to read them. Under Disposal of logs it says log data must not be destroyed before the required retention period ends, "and must not be kept beyond this time".
  • StandardThe OWASP Logging Vocabulary Cheat Sheet "proposes a standard vocabulary for logging security events". It gives authn_login_success the level INFO, authn_login_fail and input_validation_fail the level WARN, and authz_fail the level CRITICAL, and says all dates "should be logged in ISO 8601 format WITH UTC offset". It is a proposal, not a standard.
  • StandardOWASP Top 10:2025 A09 lists among its failures auditable events that "are not logged or logged inconsistently", log integrity that is not protected from tampering, logs that are not monitored, and too many false positive alerts. Among its preventions: log all login, access control and server-side input validation failures "with sufficient user context to identify suspicious or malicious accounts", and encode log data correctly. It is an awareness document and sets no requirement.
  • StandardNIST SP 800-92 (September 2006) section 5.1.3 says users should not have access to most log files beyond append-only privileges where they must create entries, that logging should be configured not to record unneeded sensitive data such as passwords, and that protecting archived logs "could include creating and securing message digests for the files". Section 5.5 lists ensuring "that each system's clock is synched to a common time source" among operational duties.
  • StandardNIST SP 800-61r3 (April 2025) section 2.1 replaces the four-phase life cycle of the previous revision with a model based on the six CSF 2.0 Functions, in which Detect, Respond and Recover are the incident response itself and Govern, Identify and Protect are preparation. It recommends that organizations use the model that suits them best. In Table 3 it recommends tuning monitoring to reduce false positives and false negatives (DE.CM), declaring incidents against defined criteria (DE.AE-08), triaging and validating each report (RS.MA-02) and determining the sequence of events (RS.AN-03).
  • StandardRFC 5424 section 6.2.1 requires a syslog Severity value to be in the range 0 to 7 and lists the names, from Emergency (0) to Debug (7), in a table. It says the Facility and Severity values "are not normative but often used" and that the tables are there "for purely informational purposes". The Logging Cheat Sheet's example of a severity scale uses the same numbers. Section 8.2 warns that an attacker may include control characters in a message.
  • StandardFor agents, the OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet, section 6, recommends: "Log all agent decisions, tool calls, and outcomes." The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, ASI02, says: "Maintain immutable logs of all tool invocations and parameter changes."
  • BaselineLog every refusal an authentication, authorization or validation control makes, with the account, the object, the route and a request id. A success-only log hides the attacks your controls stopped.
  • BaselineWrite each event as one JSON object per line through an encoder. Do not build log lines by joining strings, and do not strip characters by hand.
  • BaselinePut an allowlist of field names in the logger. Validate identifiers before logging them, and log the name of a field that failed validation, not its value.
  • BaselineKeep the event name in a field of its own and its parameters in separate fields. Treat the level as a ranking, and let rules decide who is told.
  • BaselineRun at least these rules: refusals per account in a short window, the same in a long window, different accounts failing sign-in from one address, and a count on each sensitive business flow. Replay the attack after every threshold change.
  • BaselineFor an agent, record which agent acted, on whose behalf, which tool it called and the outcome.
  • BaselineReport "no rule fired", with the rules and the rate below which each is silent. Never report "no attack".
  • OptionA hash chain over log entries, with the latest digest stored where the log's writer cannot reach. It shows an edit or a deletion. It does not prevent one.
  • OptionAutomatic blocking when a rule fires. The Logging Cheat Sheet warns that such an action must not become a way to deny service to other users.
  • OptionHoneytokens: records or identities that no real user touches, so that any access to them is an alert with almost no false positives. OWASP Top 10:2025 A09 suggests them.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • Refusals are logged, not only successes Every failed sign-in, authorization failure and input validation failure leaves an event. Test by sending a request that is refused and reading the log.
  • Each event says when, where, who and what, and carries a request id Timestamp, application, host, route, account, source address, event name, object, result and reason. The request id also appears in the error response.
  • No credential, token or session identifier is written to any log The logger has an allowlist of field names. Test with a generated password and a generated token on the failure paths, then search every log for them.
  • A logged value cannot forge or alter an entry Events are written by an encoder for a structured format. Test a value containing a line feed, a carriage return and the delimiter, and parse the log back.
  • Event names and levels come from one documented vocabulary Every service uses the same name for the same event, so one rule covers all of them.
  • Detection rules read the events, and each is tested by replaying the attack At least refusals per account, different accounts failing from one source, and a count on each sensitive business flow. Replay after every threshold change.
  • The slow and the distributed variants have been considered A long-window rule exists, and the rate below which no rule fires is written down.
  • Logs are protected from the systems that write them Append-only or copied off the host promptly, read access restricted and itself logged, and a retention period defined for each log type.
  • Clocks are synchronised to a common source The allowed clock error is smaller than the shortest window any rule uses. Timestamps carry a UTC offset.
  • An alert reaches a person who has a written procedure The procedure covers triage, the criteria for declaring an incident, reconstruction from the log, containment and what to record. It has been exercised.

checks.title: Refusals are logged, not only successes
checks.detail: Every failed sign-in, authorization failure and input validation failure leaves an event. Test by sending a request that is refused and reading the log.

checks.title: Each event says when, where, who and what, and carries a request id
checks.detail: Timestamp, application, host, route, account, source address, event name, object, result and reason. The request id also appears in the error response.

checks.title: No credential, token or session identifier is written to any log
checks.detail: The logger has an allowlist of field names. Test with a generated password and a generated token on the failure paths, then search every log for them.

checks.title: A logged value cannot forge or alter an entry
checks.detail: Events are written by an encoder for a structured format. Test a value containing a line feed, a carriage return and the delimiter, and parse the log back.

checks.title: Event names and levels come from one documented vocabulary
checks.detail: Every service uses the same name for the same event, so one rule covers all of them.

checks.title: Detection rules read the events, and each is tested by replaying the attack
checks.detail: At least refusals per account, different accounts failing from one source, and a count on each sensitive business flow. Replay after every threshold change.

checks.title: The slow and the distributed variants have been considered
checks.detail: A long-window rule exists, and the rate below which no rule fires is written down.

checks.title: Logs are protected from the systems that write them
checks.detail: Append-only or copied off the host promptly, read access restricted and itself logged, and a retention period defined for each log type.

checks.title: Clocks are synchronised to a common source
checks.detail: The allowed clock error is smaller than the shortest window any rule uses. Timestamps carry a UTC offset.

checks.title: An alert reaches a person who has a written procedure
checks.detail: The procedure covers triage, the criteria for declaring an incident, reconstruction from the log, containment and what to record. It has been exercised.

details.summary: The API already refuses every request for another customer's booking. Why log the refusals?
details.html:
The API already refuses every request for another customer's booking. Why log the refusals?

Because a refusal tells only the attacker. The walk in the lab is refused 38 times and leaves nothing in a log of successes, so it can continue against every other route until it finds one where the check is missing. The refusals are also the record an investigation starts from: which account, which identifiers, from when to when.

details.summary: The vocabulary gives authz_fail the level CRITICAL. Should each one page the on-call engineer?
details.html:
The vocabulary gives authz_fail the level CRITICAL. Should each one page the on-call engineer?

No. The level ranks the event. A customer who mistypes one booking id produces a CRITICAL event, and check 15 shows no alert for them. A rule over the events decides whether a person is told: here, five for one account inside 60 seconds.

details.summary: A colleague fixes log injection by deleting line feeds from user names before logging. What is left?
details.html:
A colleague fixes log injection by deleting line feeds from user names before logging. What is left?

The delimiters, and every other character a reader treats as a line break. Exercise 2 measures both: the forged entry disappears, the real entry now names the wrong user, and a carriage return forges the entry again. The fix is an encoder for the output format, such as one JSON object per line, not a list of characters to remove.

details.summary: No alert fired last month. What can you report?
details.html:
No alert fired last month. What can you report?
